441: C is correct because creating an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 origin offloads the delivery of high volumes of static web content from the EC2 instances to the AWS global edge network, which stops the load spikes that trigger the Auto Scaling group to launch extra On-Demand Instances. This is the most cost-effective redesign because S3 and CloudFront are inexpensive fully managed services, whereas changing the instance purchasing model still leaves the company paying for compute to serve static content.
442: D is correct because Lake Formation tag-based access control allows the data science team to assign tags to databases, tables, and columns and grant cross-account permissions based on those tags, so only the selective data the engineering team needs is shared. This sharing is managed entirely within Lake Formation across the existing multi-account data lake, avoiding data copies and per-account manual grants, and therefore meets the requirement with the least operational overhead.
443: A is correct because Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration uses Amazon CloudFront edge locations to speed up uploads and downloads of large objects over long distances, minimizing latency for globally distributed users transferring unique data up to gigabytes in size. S3 is also a highly scalable, cost-effective managed service that handles both uploads and downloads, whereas CacheControl headers, ElastiCache, or regional EC2 architectures do not accelerate large-object transfers across the globe.
444: B is correct because updating the DB instance to Multi-AZ provides a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone for high availability, and enabling deletion protection prevents the accidental deletion that caused the 24-hour outage. Placing the EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in an EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones removes the single-AZ single-point-of-failure and makes the compute tier self-healing. Together these changes maximize reliability for both the database and web tiers.
445: A is correct because AWS DataSync efficiently moves 700 TB over the existing 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection into an S3 bucket using optimized, parallel, incremental transfer, easily completing within the 90-day window. DataSync keeps the on-premises data in place and accessible during the transfer and can resync changes made during the window, so the move is efficient and non-disruptive, unlike shipping devices or an unmanaged rsync copy.
446: D is correct because S3 Object Lock in compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting objects before the 7-year retention period expires, satisfying the legal retention requirement. S3 Batch Operations can apply the retention settings to all existing objects in a single bulk managed job, bringing existing data into compliance with far less operational overhead than manually recopying every object.
447: A is correct because Amazon Route 53 health checks monitor the API endpoints in each Region, and an active-active failover configuration with Route 53 routing policies directs users to healthy Regions and automatically fails over if a Region becomes unavailable. Route 53 is the global DNS service purpose-built for multi-Region routing, whereas CloudFront has no health-based regional routing, and transit gateways or a regional load balancer cannot route global client traffic across Regions.
448: C is correct because the single customer gateway device in the data center is the single point of failure for the Management VPC's VPN connectivity. Adding a second set of VPNs from a second customer gateway device provides redundant hardware and tunnels so a single device failure does not sever connectivity. The Production VPC is already redundant with two Direct Connect connections, and extra peering connections or a second virtual private gateway would not address the failing VPN device.
449: B is correct because Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle provides a managed database service while also allowing privileged access to the underlying operating system and database, so the third-party database features requiring privileged access can continue to run. This offloads database administration, backups, and infrastructure maintenance from the company's limited resources, and unlike self-managing Oracle on EC2 it does so without the company bearing the full administrative and licensing-management burden.
450: C is correct because refactoring the three-tier application into separate web, application, and database tiers across two Availability Zones with Auto Scaling for the stateless tiers aligns with the Well-Architected pillars of scalability, resiliency, and security through layered subnets. E is correct because Elastic Load Balancers in front of the web tier distribute traffic across instances and AZs, and security groups that reference each layer's security groups enforce least-privilege communication between tiers. F is correct because a Multi-AZ RDS deployment in private subnets provides automatic failover resiliency for the database, and allowing access only from application tier security groups secures the data tier.
451: B is correct because creating the Amazon RDS DB instance and configuring its scheduled maintenance window is a customer responsibility, as instance configuration belongs to the consumer layer of the shared responsibility model. C is correct because on Amazon ECS the customer manages the software running on its containers and cluster, including additional monitoring, patch management, log management, and host intrusion detection components. F is correct because encrypting data in transit through Direct Connect is the customer's responsibility, since AWS manages the network but the customer must configure and enforce encryption of its own traffic. AWS manages the RDS infrastructure layer, OS, platform, database patching, and physical data center security.
452: B is correct because AWS Lambda is serverless and billed only for execution time, so an hourly 10-second job pays for about 10 seconds of compute per hour instead of an always-on EC2 instance. With 1 GB of memory matching the job's need and an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule triggering it each hour, the job runs with no idle cost and no instance management. Container options on ECS still run and bill continuously, and stopping and restarting the EC2 instance adds operational complexity without eliminating cost.
453: D is correct because AWS Backup provides a centrally managed backup plan covering both EC2 data and the multiple S3 buckets, and a backup vault lock in compliance mode makes the retention settings immutable so that no one, including administrators, can delete or alter the backup files before the retention period ends. Governance mode can be bypassed by privileged users, so compliance mode is required to satisfy the regulatory requirement that files cannot be altered.
454: C is correct because Workload Discovery on AWS automatically inventories resources across multiple AWS accounts and Regions and generates live architecture diagrams showing the relationships between the workloads, which is the most operationally efficient way to build and map the inventory left undocumented by the previous employee. It requires no custom orchestration or manual diagram building, unlike Step Functions or X-Ray, which would demand significant effort and only trace individual requests.
455: B is correct because AWS Budgets are created under the Billing dashboards of the required accounts, letting the company set a different budget amount for each account and track spend against it. D is correct because budget actions must run under an IAM role with the required permissions so AWS Budgets can take action on the company's behalf when a threshold is met, whereas an IAM user is not the recommended identity for service automation. F is correct because adding an alert notifies the company when a threshold is reached, and a budget action that attaches an SCP through the created IAM identity prevents the accounts from provisioning additional resources once the budget is exceeded.
456: C is correct because AWS Backup provides a single centrally managed backup plan with cross-Region copy that automatically backs up the EC2 instances to the second Region, meeting the backup and central management requirements with minimal effort. Since the second Region only needs backups until resources are provisioned, this is far cheaper than running a duplicate DR environment, and manual periodic EBS snapshot copies require more administration without central management.
457: C is correct because AWS Transfer Family supports the AS2 protocol for securely transferring data with encryption and message integrity, which is required for communication with the product manufacturer. AWS Transfer Family also supports custom identity providers, so an AWS Lambda function can authenticate application users against the company's own IdP during transfers. The other transfer services do not support the AS2 protocol requirement.
458: B is correct because AWS Lambda provides the 1 GB of memory needed for computation, integrates natively with Amazon API Gateway for the REST API, and is fully serverless, minimizing administrative effort. C is correct because Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service that satisfies the requirement for relational data with minimal administration. Lambda's ephemeral storage and RDS storage cover the 2 GB storage need, whereas EC2, DynamoDB, and EKS demand far more management or do not fit the relational and serverless requirements.
459: A is correct because the department tag is a user-defined cost allocation tag, and cost allocation tags must be activated from the billing console of the Organizations management account so they apply to cost data across all accounts in the organization. Once activated, the accounting team can create a single Cost Explorer report grouped by the department tag and filtered by EC2, identifying which departments are responsible for EC2 costs regardless of which AWS account incurred them.
460: C is correct because Amazon AppFlow is a fully managed integration service with a native Salesforce connector that transfers data directly to Amazon S3, and it supports encryption in transit as well as encryption at rest using AWS KMS customer managed keys. This meets both security requirements with no code to write or infrastructure to manage, whereas Lambda, Step Functions, or a custom connector would require custom development and ongoing maintenance.
